subtype: Approach: keeps closing the nearest gap and never steps back to check the route [Pitfall]
passage: Faculty note, capstone project review. Arohi's team had one main requirement: a working route planner that suggests the cheapest bus route. At Monday's check-in Arohi was fixing a crash on the login page. By Wednesday the login worked, but a slide looked crooked, so Arohi spent the afternoon on slide design. On Friday it was font sizes across the report. Each fix was real and took hours, yet nobody had run the route suggestion since the first week. Jasleen, a teammate, raised it quietly. Arohi said, 'I'll get to it after this.' On demo day the planner returned the wrong route. I asked Arohi to sit with me afterwards and list what the project was meant to do.

qa.q: What was the team's main requirement?
qa.a: The main requirement was a working route planner that suggests the cheapest bus route.

qa.q: What might Arohi have been feeling as each new fix seemed urgent?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt busy and pressed, and comforted by the sense of progress from each fix, without noticing the drift from the main requirement.

qa.q: What could Arohi do each day to avoid drifting?
qa.a: Arohi could step back each morning, compare the project with the main requirement, and choose the next step that closes the biggest gap to it.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when raising the route planner?
qa.a: Jasleen was probably worried but hesitant, since the point was raised quietly and then put off.

grounding: Shows a student fixing the loudest problem each time, first a bug, then a slide, then formatting, and drifting from the main requirement until the deadline.

subtype: Approach: notices a dead end and sets a temporary detour subgoal [Revision]
passage: In the analytics team's room, Dhruv had spent two hours on one error: the mapping library refused to install on the office laptop, whatever version Dhruv tried. The report was due by evening. Dhruv stopped typing and looked at the wall clock. 'I'm pushing on a closed door,' Dhruv said quietly. The question changed: not how to install it here, but where it would run. Dhruv asked Deepak, the senior engineer, for the team's container setup and spent forty minutes building one. The library installed on the first try inside it. Dhruv returned to the original gap, three missing charts, and finished them there. Deepak said the laptop's own setup could wait until Monday.

qa.q: How long did building the container take?
qa.a: Building the container took forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking when saying 'I'm pushing on a closed door'?
qa.a: Dhruv realised that repeating the install was going nowhere, and felt stuck and pressed by the evening deadline.

qa.q: What other approach could Dhruv have tried earlier?
qa.a: Dhruv could have asked Deepak sooner, or looked for a different mapping library, since a colleague may know a route around the block.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Dhruv's request for the container setup?
qa.a: Deepak probably sees a colleague who stepped back instead of losing more hours, and would be glad to share the setup.

grounding: Shows an engineer stuck on a library that will not install, setting a subgoal of using a container, and returning to the original gap once the environment works.

subtype: Approach: tries the same action in different ways until something works [Action]
passage: Nursery note. Baljeet, two, sat on the mat with the shape box and pushed the round block at the square hole. It did not go. Baljeet turned it over and pushed again, then pressed harder with both hands and grunted. Then Baljeet tried the round hole, and the block dropped in with a clunk. Baljeet clapped and looked up at me. I only smiled. Preeti, sitting beside, tried the same block in the square hole and laughed.

qa.q: What sound did the block make?
qa.a: The block dropped in with a clunk.

qa.q: How did Baljeet seem to feel when the block dropped in?
qa.a: Baljeet seemed pleased and proud, clapping and looking up at the adult.

qa.q: What could the caregiver do next time Baljeet is stuck?
qa.a: The caregiver could let Baljeet keep trying and give a small hint only if Baljeet gets upset.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen what Baljeet did?
qa.a: Preeti was probably curious, since Preeti tried the same block in the square hole and laughed.

grounding: Shows a toddler trying a round block in a square hole by turning it and pressing harder, then moving to the round hole where it drops in.

subtype: Approach: tests several options and remembers which worked [Thinking]
passage: Monday: Sona folded a paper boat the way Papa showed her and floated it in the bucket. It tipped over. Tuesday: she folded a second boat with a pointy bottom. It tipped over too. Wednesday: she folded a third with a flat, wide bottom and set it in the bucket. It sat up straight and floated. 'This one!' she said. From then on Sona folded the wide-bottomed boat every time, and she showed her cousin Nazia how.

qa.q: Which of Sona's boats stayed upright?
qa.a: The boat with the flat, wide bottom stayed upright.

qa.q: How did Sona feel when the third boat floated?
qa.a: Sona felt delighted, shown by her shout of 'This one!'

qa.q: What could Sona try next?
qa.a: Sona could fold a wide-bottomed boat with taller sides and float it in the bucket again to see if it still stays up.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt being shown the folding?
qa.a: Nazia was probably interested and pleased to learn a boat that does not tip.

grounding: Shows a child trying three ways of folding a paper boat, floating each in a bucket, and folding the wide-based one from then on.

subtype: Approach: makes small changes one at a time and watches the result [Action]
passage: Saturday: Rohan's kite kept spinning in circles. He added a longer tail and flew it once. It still wobbled, but it spun less. Sunday: he changed only the place where the string was tied, a finger-width lower, and flew it again. It leaned and dipped. 'Wrong way,' he said, and put it back. Monday: he left the string where it was and made the tail longer still, and now the kite stood steady over the field. His sister Sudha asked why he never changed both at once. 'Then I wouldn't know which one helped,' said Rohan. He wrote 'long tail = steady' on the reel.

qa.q: What did Rohan change on Sunday?
qa.a: On Sunday Rohan changed only the place where the string was tied.

qa.q: What was Rohan thinking when he changed only one thing per flight?
qa.a: Rohan wanted to know which change caused the result, so he kept everything else the same.

qa.q: What could Rohan do to learn even faster?
qa.a: Rohan could ask Sudha to watch from the ground and say which way the kite leans, since a second pair of eyes helps him see what he cannot.

qa.q: How might Sudha have seen Rohan's way of testing?
qa.a: Sudha was probably puzzled at first and then impressed, since the one-at-a-time method gave a clear answer.

grounding: Shows a boy changing the kite tail and the string position one at a time on separate flights and learning that the longer tail steadies it.

subtype: Approach: random changes with no record of what was tried [Pitfall]
passage: In a small town in Bihar, Arjun's phone crawled on the home Wi-Fi the night before his online form was due. He opened the settings and began flipping things: the network band, power saving, a network reset, the DNS, airplane mode. Nothing seemed to help, so he kept going. At some point the phone stopped connecting at all. He couldn't remember what he had changed, or in which order, and next morning had to take it to his cousin Wasim, who fixed phones at the market. Wasim asked, 'What did you touch?' Arjun shrugged. The form deadline passed, and the phone needed a full reset.

qa.q: Who did Arjun take the phone to in the morning?
qa.a: Arjun took it to his cousin Wasim, who fixed phones at the market.

qa.q: How might Arjun have felt when Wasim asked 'What did you touch?'
qa.a: Arjun probably felt embarrassed and frustrated, since he could only shrug and had missed the deadline.

qa.q: What could Arjun have done differently that night?
qa.a: Arjun could have changed one setting at a time and written it down, undoing any change that did not help.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the situation?
qa.a: Wasim probably finds it hard to help, since there is no way to tell which change caused the fault, so a full reset is the only option.

grounding: Shows a teenager flipping settings at random on a slow phone, forgetting which he changed and ending up worse off without notes.

subtype: Approach: switches to noting each attempt and its outcome [Revision]
passage:
Thursday night: Vikas changed a line, ran the program, changed another, ran it, until two in the morning. It crashed differently each time, and he lost track of what he had edited.

Friday: Sunaina, his lab partner, looked at the screen and asked, 'What did you change since it last worked?' He couldn't say. He opened a notebook and wrote three column headings: Attempt, Change, Result. Then he restored the last working copy.

Saturday: Change one, rename a variable, result: same. Change two, swap the loop order, result: crash moves earlier. Change three, print the list length before the loop, result: zero. The file reader was failing quietly. He fixed the file path and the program ran. It had taken twenty minutes.

qa.q: How long did it take to find the fault once Vikas kept the log?
qa.a: It took twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel at two in the morning after losing track of his edits?
qa.a: Vikas felt frustrated and confused, since the program crashed differently each time and he could not tell why.

qa.q: What other approach could Vikas use to track his changes?
qa.a: Vikas could save each change as a small step in a version-control tool, since it records what changed and allows going back.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen the first night of random edits?
qa.a: Sunaina probably saw guesswork that was hard to trace, which is why Sunaina asked what had changed since it last worked.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a night of random edits, starts noting each change and its result and finds the fault within twenty minutes.

subtype: Approach: uses safe cheap trials when testing is inexpensive and mistakes are recoverable [Thinking]
passage: With a tight food budget and one gas ring in the shared flat, Harsha, who had just started cooking for her flatmates, could not afford a ruined big batch of dal. So she filled four small pots with a cup of dal each and changed one thing in each: an extra pinch of turmeric, a little more cumin, lemon at the end, a tempering of garlic. Ankita, a flatmate, tasted each from a steel spoon and said, 'Number three.' Harsha wrote on the back of an envelope: cumin plus garlic. Pots one and four went into lunch boxes so nothing was wasted. Next day Harsha made a full pot with that mix and it tasted right.

qa.q: How many small pots did Harsha fill?
qa.a: Harsha filled four small pots.

qa.q: What was Harsha afraid of when choosing small pots?
qa.a: Harsha was afraid of ruining a big batch on a tight budget, so she wanted cheap trials that could be undone.

qa.q: What other approach could Harsha use to remember the recipe?
qa.a: Harsha could measure the spices in spoonfuls and write the amounts down, since a written recipe makes the good pot easy to repeat.

qa.q: How might Ankita have seen the tasting?
qa.a: Ankita probably enjoyed being part of it, and gave a clear choice by saying 'Number three.'

grounding: Shows a new cook trying spice changes in several small pots of dal instead of one big batch, so mistakes are cheap and reversible.

subtype: Approach: picks the first option that is good enough and stops looking [Thinking]
passage: Mummy's note. Nikita needed a cover for her new maths notebook before Monday. At the stationery shop the shelf held many: cartoon ones, plain brown ones, shiny ones. I braced for a long hour. Nikita took the first plain brown one, held it against the notebook, checked that it fit and wasn't torn, and said, 'This one will do.' The shopkeeper asked if she wanted to see the others. Nikita shook her head. 'It only has to fit and not be torn,' she said. We were out in five minutes, and she covered the book that evening while her brother Akash was still choosing between two erasers.

qa.q: How did Nikita decide the cover was right?
qa.a: Nikita held it against the notebook and checked that it fit and wasn't torn.

qa.q: What did Nikita want from the cover?
qa.a: Nikita wanted only a cover that fits and is not torn, and she was content with the first one that did.

qa.q: When might it be worth looking at more covers?
qa.a: It might be worth looking longer if the cover had to last all year in a crowded school bag, since then a few more checks could matter.

qa.q: How might Nikita's mother have felt?
qa.a: Nikita's mother was probably relieved and a little surprised, having braced for a long hour and been finished in five minutes.

grounding: Shows a girl taking the first plain notebook cover that fits and is not torn instead of checking every shelf at the stationery shop.

subtype: Approach: sets a minimum standard in advance and chooses the first option that meets it [Action]
passage: Sarita, you asked why I never waste hours choosing. My brother Imran taught me, at sixteen, before his board exams. He needed a place to study, and before going anywhere he wrote three rules on his hand: quiet, a table, and ten minutes from home. The first place he tried, the tea stall, was noisy. The second, the small library behind the post office, had a silent room, a long table, and took nine minutes to walk. He sat down at once. I asked, 'Aren't you going to check a third?' He said, 'It does the job. I'll lose more hours looking.' He studied there all winter. I'm Salma, and I still write my rules first.

qa.q: Which place did Imran try first, and why did it fail?
qa.a: Imran tried the tea stall first, and it failed because it was noisy.

qa.q: What was Imran thinking when Salma asked if he would check a third place?
qa.a: Imran felt sure the library was good enough and worried that more searching would cost him study hours.

qa.q: Which choice saved Imran time, and why?
qa.a: Writing the three rules first saved time, since the library met them all and he could stop looking.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt watching Imran sit down at once?
qa.a: Salma was probably surprised at first and then impressed, since Salma still writes rules first.

grounding: Shows a teenager setting a minimum standard for a study spot in advance and choosing the first place that meets it.
